title: Free Fall
short: Without air resistance, every dropped object speeds up by 9.8 m/s each second, whatever its mass.
trouble: Students think heavier objects fall faster.

blocks.html: Drop anything and, if air resistance is small, it falls with the same constant acceleration. From Mass and Weight, the gravitational force on a mass $m$ is $mg$; Newton's second law gives its acceleration as that force divided by the same mass.
In free fall every object accelerates downward at $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, whatever its mass. With up as positive, $a = -9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, and the constant-acceleration equations apply.

A heavier object is pulled harder, but it also has more inertia to overcome, in exactly the same proportion: $\role{acceleration}{a} = \dfrac{\role{force}{F}}{\role{mass}{m}} = \dfrac{\role{mass}{m}\role[acceleration of gravity]{acceleration}{g}}{\role{mass}{m}} = \role[acceleration of gravity]{acceleration}{g}$. The mass cancels. In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the airless Moon, and they landed together.

blocks.title: Signs with up positive
blocks.q: Take up as $+y$. A ball is dropped from rest. Find its velocity and displacement after $2\ \text{s}$.

blocks.html: Thinking heavier objects fall faster. In everyday life a feather drifts because air resistance matters for it, not because it is light. Without air (or when air resistance is small, as for two steel balls), objects of any mass fall together. Check: $g$ never has a mass in it.
Try it in the Science Lab: the Second Law page lets you change the mass and the force and watch the acceleration.
